name: Abilities
content:
ABILITIES are special capabilities that set characters apart from one another. Abilities encompass a very wide range of effects and mechanics, but all are defined within a shared set of concepts:

ACTION COST

An ability's ACTION COST defines when and how it can be used:

  • Trait. A passive ability that is always in effect. Traits themselves do not require activation, but may contain effects within their descriptions that require activation and/or have costs.

  • Action. Requires spending one action on your turn to activate.

  • Half Action. Requires spending one half action on your turn to activate.

  • Free Action. Can be activated at any time on your turn, without spending any actions or reactions.

  • Reaction. Activated in response to a specific triggering event defined in the ability's description. Reactions can be used at any time, regardless of whose turn it is. See Reactions below.

  • Ritual. Requires extended time and preparation to perform, as specified in the ability's description.

Abilities with a REACTION action cost include a TRIGGER statement in their description. When the trigger event occurs, the you may use that ability immediately, even if it is not your turn. Triggers appear at the top of the description in the form: "Trigger: [event]." If you have multiple reactions available, they may be spent on separate triggering events, or on multiple reactions to a single event. Any number of creatures may react to the same triggering event — each spends their own reaction independently, and the effects are resolved in "last in, first out" order.

MP COST

Most abilities come from your Mestiere, or adventuring discipline (see the Character Creation section). Just as each Mestiere varies in its approach to adventuring and the skills it leverages, MESTIERE POINTS (MP) represent different concepts for each Mestiere: physical momentum, chaos on the battlefield, arcane energy, force of will, spiritual vitality - all of these concepts are abstracted as Mestiere Points, the resource that powers many abilities.

Many abilities have a cost — an amount of MP that must be spent to activate them. If an ability has no MP cost listed, it costs nothing to activate beyond its action cost.

How a character generates and manages MP depends on their Mestiere (see the Character Creation section).

DURATION & CONCENTRATION

Some abilities' effects are instantaneous, while others have a specified DURATION. Yet other effects require CONCENTRATION to maintain.

DURATION

  • If an ability defines a duration for an effect without requiring concentration (see below), the effects lasts for the stated duration once it is put in place.

  • If an ability does not define a duration for an effect, the effect is instantaneous.

Most descriptions of duration are self explanatory: "For the next minute," "For up to 1 hour," etc.

Some effects indicate a duration in units of "rounds." This refers to rounds of combat, and is linked to the turn during which the effect is put into place:

Example 1: On your turn, you activate an effect that lasts for 1 round. That effect remains in place until the beginning of your next turn.

Example 2: During an opponent's turn, you spend a reaction to activate an effect that lasts for for 1 round. That effect remains in place until the beginning of that opponent's next turn (regardless of who the effect targets).

Example 3: You activate an effect that lasts for 3 rounds on your turn. That effect remains in place until the beginning of your third turn after this one.

Note that, because combatants can choose to order their turns as they like within their group (see the Combat section), there are often strategic considerations to make when effects with round-length durations are in play.

CONCENTRATION

Some abilities are marked CONCENTRATION with a maximum duration — for example, "Concentration, up to 1 minute." A concentration ability's effect persists for as long as it is actively sustained, up to the stated duration.

Sustaining a concentration effect costs one half action on each of your turns. It is possible to sustain any number of multiple concentration effects simultaneously, as long as you have the actions available to do so.

If you take damage while sustaining any number of effects with concentration, roll Fortitude against a difficulty equal to the total damage taken. On a pass, you continue concentrating. On a failure, all concentration effects immediately end.

Additionally, concentration ends immediately under any of the following conditions:

  • You choose to end it, as a free action.

  • You suffer any amount of Injury.

  • You suffer a Bout of Madness.

FREQUENCY LIMITS

Ability descriptions often include a FREQUENCY LIMIT on use:

  • Once per round. Resets at the start of your next turn.

  • Once per rest. Resets after either a short rest or a long rest.

  • Once per day. Resets at each sunrise.

  • Once per Quest. Resets only at the start of a new Quest.

THE "VS" NOTATION

When an ability description calls for a skill check, it uses this notation to indicate how the check should be resolved:

"[skill] vs [target]"

The left side is always a skill, to be rolled by the character using the ability. The target can be one of two different options:

  • When the target is a skill (e.g., "Strength vs Dexterity"), it is a contest, and the outcome is described as a win or loss.

  • When the target is a stat or other fixed value (e.g., "Strength vs Defense"), it is a standard skill check, with a difficulty equal to the stat or other value on the right, which is always a value belonging to the target (in the example, the target's current Defense score).

Whenever an Ability indicates multiple targets - for example, "Roll Spirit vs Dexterity against each creature within short range" - that always means that the character invoking the Ability rolls their Skill once and compares that result against each of the targets' roll results (contest) or stats (standard skill check), one at a time.

WIN, LOSS, PASS & FAIL

Ability descriptions use this terminology when referring to check outcomes:

  • Pass / Fail. Used when a skill check is made against a difficulty. Pass means the result met or exceeded the difficulty; fail means it did not. Often this is rendered as "On a pass..." or "On a failure..."

  • Win / Lose. Used when a check is a contest. Win means your result was higher than your opponent's; lose means it was lower. Often this is rendered as "On a win..." or "On a loss..."

"Win" or "loss" in an ability description is always written from your perspective. Consider this example:

"Roll Spirit vs Dexterity against a creature within short range. On a win, the creature takes 2d6 damage. On a loss, half damage."

In this case, you roll Spirit and the creature you chose rolls Dexterity. If you win the contest, the creature takes 2d6 damage. If you lose the contest, the creature takes half of that damage.

"Pass" and "fail" are used more flexibly. In some cases, they refer to the outcome of a roll you make against a fixed value. In others, they refer to the outcome of a roll a target makes against a fixed value. Descriptions are written to make it clear who is passing or failing.

DIFFICULTY

Some abilities set and use a special, variable DIFFICULTY as part of an ongoing effect. Typically this is a value that you set when you activate the ability - e.g. "roll Spirit to set the Difficulty." This usually represents an initial effort you make, which another creature may later attempt to overcome by rolling against it.

For example, you might place a magical lock on a door, rolling a skill to set the Difficulty. Later, a creature might try to open the magically locked door, rolling another skill against the Difficulty to see if it succeeds.

In a sense, Difficulty is essentially a method for determining a contest across a span of time - storing the result of one roll so that it can later be compared to an opposing roll.

Ability descriptions simply refer to "the Difficulty." This always means the Difficulty for this ability in particular, not the Difficulty for any other abilities or checks.

In the app, abilities that call for setting a Difficulty have a diamond-shaped space at the top of their card that allows you to store a value for that ability's Difficulty.

BIOME INFLUENCE

Some abilities - chiefly those of the Wildheart mestiere - are strengthened or weakened by the current biome. Biome tags that strengthen or weaken a given ability are noted with icons under the "+" and "-" sections near the bottom of the ability's card.

Each biome has a set of tags associated with it. If the current biome's tags match more of an ability's "+" tags than its "-" tags, all your skill checks for that ability are favored by default, and you roll each damage die twice and keep the best result. If the current biome's tags match more of an ability's "-" tags than its "+" tags, all your skill checks for that ability are ill-favored by default, and you roll each damage die twice and keep the worst result.

IMPROVEMENTS

Some abilities offer IMPROVEMENTS — additional upgrades for that ability, each with its own description and XP cost. Owning the base ability is a prerequisite for purchasing any of its improvements. Improvements are purchased with XP, and can be purchased as a free action at any time during gameplay, just like general character improvement XP expenditure (see the Character Advancement section).

A character may purchase any number of improvements for the same ability. Each improvement stacks with the base ability and with any other improvements already purchased — improvements do not replace the base ability's effects unless otherwise stated.

OTHER RULES & TERMINOLOGY

TARGETS & VISIBILITY

When choosing a target for an ability, unless an ability specifically states otherwise, you must always choose a target you can see, whether that target is a creature, multiple creatures, a point, or multiple points.

ROUNDING

Unless otherwise stated, always round down when dividing or otherwise modifying values.

CREATURE & RELATED TERMS

Ability descriptions occasionally make use of special terms to describe certain types of beings:

  • A "creature" is any sentient being.

  • A "humanoid" is any sentient being with human-like or mostly human-like features, who has a WITS score of 1 or higher.

  • An "animal" is a non-magical creature without human-like features with a WITS score of 0.

  • An "ally" is any creature acting collaboratively with you.

  • A "foe" is any creature engaged in combat against you.

If a creature's allegiance is questionable, the GM decides whether they are an ally, foe or neutral for the purposes of a given ability.
